title: Direct synthesis of dimethyl ether from carbon-monoxide-rich synthesis gas: Influence of dehydration catalysts and operating conditions
abstract: Various dehydration catalysts were studied in the synthesis of dimethyl ether (DME) directly from carbon-monoxide-rich synthesis gas under a series of different reaction conditions. The investigated catalyst systems consisted of combinations of a methanol catalyst (CuO/ZnO system) with catalysts for methanol dehydration based on γ-Al2O3 or zeolites and γ-Al2O3 was identified as the most favorable dehydration catalyst. Various reaction parameters such as temperature, H2/CO ratio and space velocity were studied. The impact of water on Cu/ZnO/Al2O3-γ-Al2O3 catalysts was investigated and no deactivation could be observed at water contents below 10% during running times of several hours. A running time of several days and a water content of 10% led to a significant increase of CO conversion but the water gas shift reaction became dominating and CO2 was the main product. After termination of water feeding significant deactivation of the catalyst system was observed but the system returned to high DME selectivity. Catalyst stability and the influence of CO2 in the gas feed were studied in experiments lasting for about three weeks. The presence of 8% of CO2 caused an approximately 10% lower CO conversion and an about 5% lower DME selectivity compared to the reaction system without CO2.
paragraphs: Dimethyl ether (DME) is the simplest ether and a non-toxic, colorless, weakly narcotic, and easily inflammable gas under standard conditions. By moderate increase of pressure, it can be liquefied and its properties are largely similar to those of liquefied petrol gas (LPG). DME can be applied in a variety of areas and hence, interest in DME is steadily increasing. DME can be produced from various resources like coal, natural gas, or biomass. For this purpose, raw materials are first converted to synthesis gas which serves as feedstock for the production of methanol. Subsequently, methanol is dehydrated to give DME in high yields. Presently, DME is applied as an aerosol propellant in cosmetics industry or as a LPG substitute in domestic energy supply. Moreover, DME is considered as an attractive alternative fuel to replace fossil fuels in the long term. Compared to conventional diesel, for example, it has much better combustion properties and, if produced from biological residues, it might be a sustainable fuel in the future.

In light of this, a multi-stage process for the production of fuels and chemicals from biomass, the so-called bioliq® process, is currently developed. Within this process biomass is firstly pyrolyzed to a slurry, which is subsequently converted to synthesis gas employing an entrained-flow high-pressure gasifier. This biomass-based synthesis gas is characterized by a comparatively high CO content (H2/CO≤1). The downstream synthesis steps are preceded by hot-gas cleaning to remove impurities from the synthesis gas without influencing the H2/CO ratio. The first synthesis step implies direct conversion of synthesis gas to DME (Syngas-To-DME, STD), without isolation of intermediary formed methanol, and the entire process is completed by conversion of thus obtained DME to gasoline (DME-To-Gasoline, DTG).

Bifunctional catalyst systems, comprising a catalyst for methanol formation as well as a catalyst for in situ methanol dehydration to DME, can be employed for direct STD conversion and the following reactions can take place simultaneously: (1) 2 CO+4 H2 ⟶2 CH3OH ΔH=−182.2kJ/mol (2) 2 CH3OH⟶CH3OCH3 +H2O ΔH=−23.5kJ/mol (3) CO+H2O⟶H2 +CO2 ΔH=−41.2kJ/mol.
The overall reaction is: (4) 3 CO+3 H2 ⟶CH3OCH3 +CO2 ΔH=−246.9kJ/mol.

As methanol synthesis (1), methanol dehydration (2), and water–gas shift reaction (WGSR) (3) can be coupled in a single reactor, CO-rich synthesis gas, ideally with a H2/CO ratio of 1, can be used for direct conversion to DME as outlined in Eq. (4). Since no separate WGSR reactor is needed, costs can be reduced. Moreover, CO conversion is more efficient, because the equilibrium limitation of methanol synthesis can be minimized. According to the state of the art, direct DME synthesis is performed in slurry or fixed-bed reactors. Regarding catalysts, classical Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 systems for low pressure methanol synthesis can be employed and such systems can also catalyze the water–gas shift reaction. Dehydration of methanol can be efficiently performed using solid-acid catalysts and typical examples are zeolites, mixed oxides, modified alumina or simply γ-Al2O3. The latter is very attractive inasmuch as it is cost-efficient and it exhibits high activity, high chemical as well as thermal stability and, due to the comparatively low content of highly acidic sites, high selectivity towards DME.

Development of direct DME synthesis is already on an advanced stage and feasibility is ascertained, even on industrial scale. However, there is still a large potential for improving and optimizing STD technology. Catalyst systems are prone to deactivation by sintering of active copper sites, coke deposition, poisoning by contaminants in the synthesis gas or adsorption of water and thus blockage of acidic sites. The presence of water in the synthesis gas feed can also affect methanol dehydration thus limiting DME formation. On the other hand, water can significantly reduce catalyst deactivation by coke formation. In light of this, resistant catalyst systems that tolerate other components such as water while maintaining activity and selectivity are highly desirable.

Within this work, a bench-scale fixed-bed reactor was employed to study DME synthesis directly from CO-rich synthesis gas (H2/CO≤1). Catalyst mixtures consisting of a methanol catalyst based on CuO/ZnO and different methanol dehydration components were studied and their STD efficiency was quantified. Zeolites of the mordenite and ZSM-5 type as well as γ-Al2O3 were investigated as dehydration components. The latter was chosen because of its above-mentioned favorable characteristics and, for comparison, zeolites with strongly varying acidity were selected, ranging from highly acidic in the case of a mordenite catalyst to weakly acidic in the case of a MFI catalyst with a high Si/Al ratio. Furthermore, the influence of several reaction parameters, e.g. temperature, H2/CO ratio and space velocity was studied. The impact of water and CO2 in the gas feed was also investigated focusing on Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 as catalyst for methanol synthesis combined with γ-Al2O3 as catalyst for methanol dehydration.

Catalyst samples from several companies were applied. The methanol catalyst (Catalyst T-4611; 64% CuO, 24% ZnO and 12% Al2O3) and zeolites (H-MFI 90 with a Si/Al ratio of 45, H-MFI 400 with a Si/Al ratio of 200 and H-MOR 90 with a Si/Al ratio of 45) were obtained from Süd-Chemie AG. The WGSR catalyst BV123456 (43% CuO, 44% ZnO and 13% Al2O3) was supplied by BASF SE and γ-Al2O3 was purchased from Alfa Aesar. The catalysts were used as received, without any further modification.

The catalyst surfaces were characterized in terms of their specific surface area (BET), pore radius distribution, and mean pore radius. Measurements were carried out by N2-adsorption–desorption using a Quantachrome Nova 2200 instrument.

Acidity of the respective dehydration catalysts was determined by temperature-programmed NH3 desorption (NH3-TPD). Measurements were carried out using a TPDRO 1100 instrument from Thermo Fisher Scientific. Catalyst samples of about 200mg with particle sizes between 355 and 500μm were used. The samples were placed in a quartz glass reactor and heated under He atmosphere up to 550°C with a heating rate of 10°C/min. Subsequently, the system was cooled down to 60°C and the sample was saturated with NH3 for 60min. After rinsing the system with He for 90min, the TPD measurement was started and the sample was heated under He atmosphere to 600°C with a heating rate of 10°C/min. The TPD profile was recorded employing a thermal conductivity detector (TCD).

For direct conversion of synthesis gas to DME, a laboratory plant was designed for the use of both gaseous and liquid components (Fig. 1 ). Dosage of the gases was controlled by mass flow controllers (MFC). For liquids, e.g. H2O, a liquid mass flow controller (LiquiFlow®, LFC) was coupled with a direct evaporator (DV 2 Adrop). Reactions took place in a stainless steel fixed-bed reactor and an alloy that prevents methanation reactions was chosen. The reactor was designed for pressures of up to 10MPa and temperatures of up to 450°C. Its volume was 60.3ml, divided into three heating zones to ensure isothermal conditions. The facility operated with a process visualization system (IFix®, GE Fanuc Automation) and online analysis of the gas phase was carried out using a HP 6890 gas chromatograph from Agilent equipped with two columns (RT®-U-BOND and RT-Msieve 5A, RESTEK) and two detectors (TCD and flame ionization detector, FID).

For the determination of catalytic activities, 2g of each catalyst system (mixture of 1g of methanol and/or WGSR catalyst and 1g of dehydration catalyst) with a particle size between 355 and 500μm were fed into the reactor. The reactor was slowly heated up to 240°C under reducing atmosphere (2% H2 in Ar) with a heating rate of 17°C/h. Thereafter, the gas flow was switched to pure H2 and the temperature was increased to 250°C within 1h. After keeping the system for 2h under these conditions it was rinsed with Ar and subjected to pressure (p =5.1MPa). Finally, synthesis gas of variable H2/CO ratios was fed into the system, the desired reaction conditions were adjusted and the respective measurements were started.

The results of surface analyses of the dehydration catalysts are shown in Table 1 . In the case of γ-Al2O3, a comparatively low BET surface area of 219m2/g was found and the material does not exhibit a microporous structure (average pore diameter D p >2nm). The BET surfaces of the zeolites range from 320 to 380m2/g and all of them exhibit micropores (D p <2nm). While the total pore volumes V P of H-MFI 400 and H-MOR 90 are nearly the same, the pore volume of H-MFI 90 is higher by a factor of about 1.6. Regarding micropores, pore volumes V P,micro and the specific areas A P,micro of the zeolites decrease in the following order: H-MOR 90>H-MFI 400>H-MFI 90.

The NH3-TPD results obtained for the four different dehydration catalysts are summarized in Fig. 2 . For all samples, two peaks can be identified. The peaks at lower temperatures can be assigned to NH3 desorption from weak or moderate acid sites. The peaks at higher temperatures reflect NH3 desorption from strong acid sites. Details of the measurements can be found in Table 2 . Irrespective of their type, the total number of acid sites is highest for H-MOR 90 and catalyst acidities decrease in the following order: H-MOR 90>H-MFI 90>γ-Al2O3 >H-MFI 400. Regarding acidities of weak and moderate acidic sites, which can be deduced from the temperature shift of the peak maxima, a similar decrease is observed: H-MOR 90>H-MFI 90>H-MFI 400>γ-Al2O3. The NH3-TPD results reveal that the dehydration catalysts differ considerably in the number and acidity of the acid sites. With regard to the nature of the acidic sites several studies were carried out using e.g. FTIR spectroscopy with probe molecules such as pyridine, ammonia, hydrogen, carbon monoxide or DME. Concerning γ-Al2O3, acidity is, according to several investigations, mainly due to Lewis-acid sites [9,20–23] whereas acidity of MFI zeolites is in many cases clearly dominated by Brønsted-acid sites. Acidity of H-MOR zeolites can also be dominated by Brønsted-acid centers but H-MOR systems with an approximately equal number of Brønsted- and Lewis-acid sites were also described and both types of acid sites exhibited high acid strength.

To determine the influence of the different dehydration catalysts, these were mixed mechanically with the methanol catalyst T-4611 (w:w=1:1, m total =2g, particle size: 355–500μm) and the catalyst mixtures were activated in the reactor as described above. After this, synthesis gas was converted directly to DME. Various operation parameters were set and the H2/CO ratio, temperature as well as space velocity were varied. In all experiments, pressure (5.1MPa) and synthesis gas dilution (70% inert gas dilution) were kept constant. For inert gas dilution a mixture of Ar and N2 was used. Nitrogen was employed as internal standard and its flow was kept constant at 10mlN/min in all test settings.

The reaction temperature was varied and two H2/CO ratios, H2/CO=1 and 0.67, were investigated (Fig. 3 ). For a better interpretation and comparison of the results, equilibrium conversions were calculated using Aspen Plus® (V7.1, Aspen Technology Inc.) and these data are also shown in Fig. 3. The conversion increases with increasing temperature and, using γ-Al2O3 as dehydration catalyst, a maximum is reached at 250°C. Such a maximum cannot be found for the zeolites in the investigated temperature range. Nevertheless, since the chosen methanol catalyst is known to deactivate at temperatures above 250°C during long-term operation the study was stopped at 260°C to prevent an irreversible deactivation of the methanol catalyst due to sintering effects of the copper particles and not to endanger further studies. Assuming that catalyst deactivation can be neglected, an increase in CO conversion by temperature raise would be limited by thermodynamic equilibrium conversion.

Evaluation of the catalyst systems with respect to CO conversion (C CO) showed that their activity increases in the following order: H-MOR 90<H-MFI 90<H-MFI 400<γ-Al2O3 for temperatures below 240°C and H-MOR 90<H-MFI 400<γ-Al2O3 <H-MFI 90 for temperatures beyond 240°C. The strongly increasing CO conversion in the case of H-MFI 90 is accompanied by a significant decrease of DME selectivity and formation of hydrocarbons is significantly favored. Besides the increasing formation of hydrocarbons, the CO2 concentration in the product mixture is also considerably increasing. This can be traced back to an enhanced WGSR activity stimulated by a higher water concentration in the reaction system and leading to a pronounced production of CO2 and H2. In consequence of the increasing H2 concentration, conversion of CO to methanol is favored. Conversions of all catalyst systems decreased with decreasing H2/CO ratio and details are summarized in Table 3 . Under test conditions, high DME selectivities (SDME) were reached employing γ-Al2O3 and H-MFI 400. The system with H-MOR 90 gave lower conversions and also exhibited a lower DME selectivity. At temperatures above 250°C, highest CO conversions were reached by the combination of T-4611 with H-MFI 90. However, CO2 and higher hydrocarbons (HC) were formed rather than DME.

With increasing temperature, DME selectivity not only of the H-MFI 90 catalyst but also of the H-MOR 90 catalyst decreased abruptly and an enhanced formation of CO2 and higher hydrocarbons could be observed. The higher hydrocarbons result from further DME conversion and it should be pointed out that, especially in the case of H-MOR 90, the concentrations of hydrocarbons are considerably high given that reaction temperatures are comparatively low. The increasing CO2 formation can be explained, as mentioned above for the H-MFI 90 catalyst, by an increasing release of water and this water can react with CO to CO2 and H2 via the WGSR.

Irrespective of the catalyst system used, the selective dehydration of methanol to DME is determined by the type of acid sites and their role is discussed controversially. While weak and moderate acid sites are considered to be predominantly involved [1,33–39], Kim et al. report that in the case of the zeolite H-ZSM-5 strong acid sites are crucial for methanol dehydration and the formation of DME. With respect to aluminum oxide catalysts, it was ascertained that DME selectivity decreases and mainly olefins are formed with increasing acidity. It is known and confirmed by numerous experiments that product distribution depends on the dehydration catalysts and explanations of this phenomenon are usually based on the acidity of the catalysts. It is also reported that product distribution can be influenced selectively by the pore size of the catalysts and these results correlate with the widespread opinion that weak and moderate acid sites of the dehydration catalyst and total acidity are essential for the selective dehydration of methanol to DME.

As shown by NH3-TPD measurements (Fig. 2), γ-Al2O3 and H-MFI 400 hardly have strong acid sites. Compared to H-MFI 90 and H-MOR 90, the total number of acid sites is also considerably lower (Table 2). Both zeolites, H-MFI 90 and H-MOR 90, exhibit numerous weak acid sites and also exhibit strong acid sites. As already mentioned above, product mixtures obtained with these zeolites at temperatures above 225°C preferably consist of CO2 and higher hydrocarbons. Despite the partly similar product distributions obtained with these zeolites, the system with H-MFI 90 differs considerably from that with H-MOR 90 as far as CO conversion is concerned. Employing H-MFI 90, CO conversion at about 240°C is not only considerably higher than in the case of H-MOR 90 but also exceeded that of the two systems containing γ-Al2O3 and H-MFI 400 (Fig. 3). Regarding the methanol content obtained with H-MOR 90, this observation was surprising, as the amount of methanol in the product mixture decreased constantly at temperatures above 225°C, contrary to the catalyst system containing H-MFI 90. Hence, the equilibrium limitation of methanol synthesis should be much better by-passed by direct further reaction of the methanol formed, which should lead to higher CO conversion.

Considering the overall product distribution of both catalyst systems at a temperature of 250 or 260°C in a CO-rich atmosphere (Table 3), the following observations were made: 1. Using H-MFI 90, DME is nearly completely converted to higher hydrocarbons whereas for H-MOR 90, a DME/hydrocarbon ratio of around 0.75 is reached. The fact that H-MOR 90 converts DME only partly to hydrocarbons in spite of its higher acidity could be attributed to its pore structure. Large parts of its surface are covered by micropores (Table 1), whose accessibility is aggravated. 2. The use of H-MFI 90 preferably results in the formation of C3 hydrocarbons and small fractions of C1 and C4 hydrocarbons (C1:C3:C4 =0.2:1.0:0.2). H-MOR 90 mainly yields C2 and C1 hydrocarbons as well as small amounts of C3 and C4 hydrocarbons (C1:C2:C3:C4 =0.6:1.0:0.2:0.1). These product distributions are not completely in agreement with typical product compositions described by Chang but this might be due to different experimental conditions and the different reaction systems. 3. Employing H-MFI 90, the methanol fraction cannot be dehydrated completely. In contrast, H-MOR 90 almost completely converts the intermediate formed methanol. While comparing these two dehydration catalysts, it must be taken into account that the CO conversion of H-MFI 90 (C CO,max =53 and 40%) is considerably higher than that of H-MOR 90 (C CO,max =27 and 18%). Consequently, the catalyst system with H-MFI 90 is much more efficient and largely abolishes the equilibrium limitation of methanol synthesis. The increased performance of H-MFI 90 might be explained by its higher pore volume (Table 1) and its pore structure. The pore volume of H-MFI 90 exceeds that of H-MOR 90 by a factor of 1.6. In addition, the former exhibits a three-dimensional pore structure, which is supposed to facilitate transport processes. The residues of methanol remaining in the product mixture might result from the synthesis of C3 and C4 hydrocarbons and dehydration to C3 and C3+ takes place more slowly than dehydration to C1 and C2 products. The active centers could be blocked and not available for the immediate dehydration of newly formed methanol. 4. The catalyst system with H-MFI 90 yields, at 260°C, CO2 as the main product (DME:CO2:MeOH:HC≈0.01:1.0:0.6:0.3). Due to the high CO conversion and dehydration to C3 products, a comparatively high amount of water is generated. The three-dimensional pore system of H-MFI 90 could promote efficient water removal and availability for WGSR so that mainly CO2 is formed in the end. Catalyst H-MOR 90, by contrast, leads to a more balanced product distribution (DME:CO2:HC≈0.6:1.0:0.7). Due to its primarily one-dimensional pore structure, mass transfer might be obstructed, which would inhibit dehydration reactions and aggravate water transport to the active centers for WGSR of the methanol catalyst. Due to the favored formation of C1 and C2 products and the lower CO conversion, less water would be formed, which could react further to CO2.

Using H-MFI 90, DME is nearly completely converted to higher hydrocarbons whereas for H-MOR 90, a DME/hydrocarbon ratio of around 0.75 is reached. The fact that H-MOR 90 converts DME only partly to hydrocarbons in spite of its higher acidity could be attributed to its pore structure. Large parts of its surface are covered by micropores (Table 1), whose accessibility is aggravated.

The use of H-MFI 90 preferably results in the formation of C3 hydrocarbons and small fractions of C1 and C4 hydrocarbons (C1:C3:C4 =0.2:1.0:0.2). H-MOR 90 mainly yields C2 and C1 hydrocarbons as well as small amounts of C3 and C4 hydrocarbons (C1:C2:C3:C4 =0.6:1.0:0.2:0.1). These product distributions are not completely in agreement with typical product compositions described by Chang but this might be due to different experimental conditions and the different reaction systems.

While comparing these two dehydration catalysts, it must be taken into account that the CO conversion of H-MFI 90 (C CO,max =53 and 40%) is considerably higher than that of H-MOR 90 (C CO,max =27 and 18%). In addition, the former exhibits a three-dimensional pore structure, which is supposed to facilitate transport processes. The residues of methanol remaining in the product mixture might result from the synthesis of C3 and C4 hydrocarbons and dehydration to C3 and C3+ takes place more slowly than dehydration to C1 and C2 products. The active centers could be blocked and not available for the immediate dehydration of newly formed methanol.

The catalyst system with H-MFI 90 yields, at 260°C, CO2 as the main product (DME:CO2:MeOH:HC≈0.01:1.0:0.6:0.3). Due to the high CO conversion and dehydration to C3 products, a comparatively high amount of water is generated. The three-dimensional pore system of H-MFI 90 could promote efficient water removal and availability for WGSR so that mainly CO2 is formed in the end. Catalyst H-MOR 90, by contrast, leads to a more balanced product distribution (DME:CO2:HC≈0.6:1.0:0.7). Due to the favored formation of C1 and C2 products and the lower CO conversion, less water would be formed, which could react further to CO2.

Apart from the temperature dependence, the influence of space velocity and residence time was studied for a synthesis gas with a H2/CO ratio of 1 (Fig. 4 ). The residence time τ mod is defined as relation of catalyst bulk volume to total flow rate under reaction conditions ( τ mod = V bulk,catalyst V ˙ total,reactor ). With increasing residence time CO conversion increases in all cases. While DME selectivity decreases with increasing residence time in the case of the catalysts H-MFI 90 and H-MOR 90, it remains constant employing the catalysts γ-Al2O3 and H-MFI 400.

Detailed results obtained with respect to the influence of the residence time are summarized in Table 4 , complemented by results obtained with a H2/CO ratio of 0.67. At a H2/CO ratio of 0.67, DME selectivities of H-MFI 90 and H-MOR 90 are similar to those obtained using a H2/CO ratio of 1.0. With decreasing space velocity, DME selectivity of these systems decreases and CO2 as well as higher HC contents in the product stream increase. Employing γ-Al2O3 and H-MFI 400 as dehydration catalysts, CO conversions at a H2/CO ratio of 0.67 are significantly lower than at a H2/CO ratio of 1.0. In these cases, DME selectivity remains constantly on a high level and the main by-product is CO2.

Dependencies of product distribution on residence time can be explained by the variable acidity of the dehydration catalysts. As a result of the strongly acidic character of H-MFI 90 and H-MOR 90, their potential for converting DME further to higher hydrocarbons and water becomes more and more apparent with increasing residence time. It is assumed that the efficiency of these conversions depends on both the acidities and the pore system of the catalyst.

Production of DME by dehydration of methanol was investigated extensively and in many cases systems based on γ-Al2O3 were reported to be suitable dehydration catalysts. Results obtained within this study also indicated a good catalytic performance of γ-Al2O3. However, it was pointed out that γ-Al2O3 can deactivate rapidly if the gas feed contains significant amounts of water and this was ascribed to the blockage of acid sites on the catalyst surface by water. To elucidate this phenomenon, experiments with gas mixtures containing variable amounts of water were carried out.

For the conversion of synthesis gas to methanol, two Cu/ZnO systems were applied as catalysts, the methanol catalyst T-4611 described above and a Cu-ZnO-based WGSR catalyst. These catalysts were mixed mechanically with γ-Al2O3 and particle sizes between 355 and 500μm were adjusted. The investigated catalyst systems are summarized in Table 5 . After activation of the catalyst mixture in the reactor, a gas mixture composed of H2:CO:(Ar+H2O+N2) in a ratio of 1:1:1 with a (Ar+H2O):N2 ratio of 4:1 was fed into the reactor. After the first GC measurement, water vapor was supplied together with the synthesis gas flow. The amount of water vapor was subtracted from the argon fraction to keep the total volume flow constant. Measurements were made over periods of 4h, subsequently, water concentration was further increased (Fig. 5 ).

Using system S1, the addition of water first causes a slight increase in CO conversion at constant selectivity. If the water content exceeds 10vol.%, CO conversion increases immediately. Simultaneously, DME selectivity decreases and formation of CO2, instead of DME, is enhanced. The use of a WGSR catalyst in catalyst system S2, instead of a methanol catalyst, causes a considerably lower CO conversion. With increasing water content, DME selectivity remains constant. System S3 that combines the methanol catalyst with the WGSR catalyst enables high CO conversion and constant DME selectivity. An increasing water content comes along with a slight increase of CO conversion. Using system S4 consisting of a methanol catalyst and γ-Al2O3 at a mass ratio of 1.5:0.5, CO conversions are somewhat higher than those of S3 and also increase slightly while selectivities remain constant. Using the systems S2, S3 and S4, short-term water addition up to 25vol.% during about 1.5h did not have any negative impact on conversion and selectivity.

Hence, the addition of water directly influences the WGSR. Low amounts of water (<10vol.%) lead to a slight increase of CO conversion in all systems, without adversely affecting the DME selectivity. This effect can be explained by the fact that more H2 is formed by the WGSR and this leads to increased CO conversion. Employing catalyst system S1, methanol concentration in the product mixture increases from 0.7 to values above 2% if water addition exceeds 20vol.%, which means that the dehydration activity of γ-Al2O3 slightly decreases. This is in accordance with previous findings. However, using the systems S2, S3 and S4 with a WGSR catalyst, a combination of a WGSR and a methanol catalyst as well as a system with a higher content of methanol catalyst, respectively, methanol concentration remained nearly constant, even if large amounts of water above 20vol.% were added. This could be attributed to the fact that the WGSR in the systems S2 and S3 is ideally supported by the use of a WGSR catalyst and that water is consumed, at least partially. The same effect could explain the performance of catalyst system S4. Its high content of methanol catalyst, which also supports the WGSR, could be beneficial with respect to water removal from the catalyst system thus avoiding water accumulation and deactivation of the catalyst system.

Luan et al. studied direct DME synthesis over a period of 30h using hydrogen-rich synthesis gas and reported that the addition of about 5% water vapor at temperatures up to 240°C hardly influences the process, but higher water contents resulted in an accelerated deactivation of the copper-based catalyst (reaction conditions: T =220°C, p =2.0MPa, GHSV=4000h−1, H2:CO:N2 =30:15:1, run time of 30h; results: 0% H2O: Y DME ≈6%, 10% H2O: Y DME ≈9%, 20% H2O: Y DME ≈13%). Deactivation was attributed to sintering processes in the case of water contents above 10%. No negative impact on the dehydration components, a combination of γ-Al2O3 and H-ZSM-5, was observed. In contrast, Ereña et al. also employed hydrogen-rich synthesis gas and found that the addition of small amounts of water causes a significant decrease in DME yield (reaction conditions: T =275°C, p =4.0MPa, H2:CO=4:1, GHSV=8.33gCat. hmolreactants −1, run time of 30h; results obtained with CuO–ZnO–Al2O3/γ-Al2O3: 0mlH2O/min: Y DME decreased from approximately 20 to 10%, 0.002mlH2O/min: Y DME ≈4%, 0.004mlH2O/min: Y DME ≈2.5%; results obtained with CuO–ZnO–Al2O3/NaHZSM-5: 0mlH2O/min: Y DME decreased from approximately 28.5 to 20.5%, 0.001mlH2O/min: Y DME ≈20%, 0.002mlH2O/min: Y DME ≈3%). It becomes obvious from these controversial results that it is difficult to predict the effect of water addition, because not only type and quality of catalysts but also reaction conditions, in particular temperature and synthesis gas composition, play a decisive role.

The influence of water in slurry reactors was also studied. Kim et al. used CO-rich synthesis gas (H2/CO=1) and the catalyst was treated with water prior to the reaction. It was observed that water influences both the methanol and the dehydration catalyst and the adsorbed water blocks the active centers. On the methanol catalyst, adsorption of H2 and, hence, methanol synthesis is inhibited. With respect to the γ-Al2O3 catalyst, blockage of the acid sites by adsorbed water suppresses dehydration, which adversely affects CO conversion, as the equilibrium limitation of methanol synthesis can no longer be by-passed.

Wang et al. also focused on DME synthesis in a slurry reactor and studied the influence of water on the catalyst system. A mixture of a commercially available copper-based methanol catalyst and a commercially available γ-Al2O3 catalyst as dehydration component was employed. It was observed that the water formed during the reaction deactivates the copper catalyst to a larger extent than the γ-Al2O3 catalyst. It was found that the reaction mixtures accounted for a high load of water on the copper catalyst and this led to a rapid activity loss. Methanol synthesis in the absence of any dehydration catalyst was carried out and water was added to the system. This led at first to an increase of CO conversion followed by a strong activity loss (reaction conditions: T =260°C, p =5.0MPa, H2/CO=2, GHSV=4000h−1, H2O/synthesis gas=0.1mol/mol, run time of approximately 192h; results: without H2O: C CO decreased from approximately 38 to 31.5%, with H2O: C CO declined from approximately 42 to 27%). This strong activity loss was attributed to sintering of the active copper centers caused by water addition. Another reason for the decreasing activity of the methanol catalyst was the loss of Zn and Al2O3 due to hydrothermal leaching. It is still not clear whether these results are also applicable for the catalyst system under fixed-bed conditions. Parameswaran et al. argued that water removal from the copper surface could be more difficult in a slurry reactor, as the oil could impede this. However, results described by this group are as controversial as those obtained from experiments in fixed-bed reactors.

Within this work low water concentrations (<10%) did not lead to a rapid deactivation of the chosen catalyst systems over periods of several hours. The catalyst systems containing the methanol catalyst T-4611 and/or the shift catalyst BV123456 in combination with γ-Al2O3 showed a slight increase of CO conversion at constant selectivity while the water content was kept below 10%. With increasing water content CO conversion grew and DME selectivity decreased but any affection was reversible. However, additional experiments over significantly longer running times were also carried out. The same reaction conditions and catalyst system S1, which led to a remarkably higher CO conversion and a drop of DME selectivity at water contents higher than 10% (Fig. 5), were employed. After catalyst activation and running the reaction for 12h, a water content of 10% was adjusted in the gas mixture and the catalytic performance was monitored during 5 d. Subsequently, water feeding was stopped and the reaction was allowed to run for another 5 d in the absence of water while maintaining the same reaction conditions (Fig. 6 ). CO conversion was around 58% before water feeding and increased immediately to 75% on average in the presence of water (Fig. 6a). However, DME selectivity dropped from values clearly above 60% to approximately 30% and CO2 became the main product. Its yield increased from 31 to 64% (Fig. 6b). These results, together with the above-mentioned findings from short-term investigations, clearly indicate that the WGSR is strongly promoted in the presence of such high amounts of water and the dehydration catalyst could be less affected compared to the methanol catalyst. Methanol selectivity increased from below 1 to 2.4% but this low value was not exceeded throughout the whole experiment. After termination of water feeding the original CO conversion of 58% could not be reached again and values around 40% were observed over an operating period of 5 d. Thus, the catalyst system suffered from water loading and did not return without further ado to its initial performance. However, DME selectivity returned immediately to the initial situation and CO2 formation rapidly declined. It should be pointed out that a sudden addition of a comparatively high amount of water (Fig. 6) results in a rapid change of conversion and selectivity whereas a successive addition (Fig. 5) leads to a significantly slower change.

The stability of the T-4611/γ-Al2O3 catalyst system was studied in long-term experiments lasting for about three weeks. In this context, the influence of CO2 on the process was also evaluated and investigations were carried out with 8% and without CO2 in the gas feed (Fig. 7 ). For both gas compositions similar effects were observed. CO conversions decreased significantly within the first days and the T-4611/γ-Al2O3 catalyst reached stationary performance after about 400h. The presence of CO2 resulted in an approximately 10% lower CO conversion compared to the reaction system without CO2. This lower CO conversion was observed throughout the whole experiment. Concerning DME selectivity, values remained constant and high. In the absence of CO2, selectivities around 70% were observed and slightly lower values of around 65% were found in the presence of CO2.

Similar results were also reported by other research groups in particular for methanol synthesis. For instance, Kung reported that in microreactor studies, depending on the catalyst amount and reaction conditions, stationary performance was reached after an operating time of 1 to 20h. The initial decrease of activity, which could reach up to 60%, was ascribed to a loss of active surface by agglomeration of highly dispersed copper crystallites. Structural modifications of Cu/ZnO catalysts in the presence of synthesis gas were observed by Topsøe and Helveg et al. employing in situ characterization techniques, e.g. high resolution transmission electron microscopy. Such structural changes together with catalyst poisoning by blockage of active sites are certainly among the main reasons for deactivation of methanol catalysts. The observed decrease of CO conversion (Fig. 7) is in accordance with findings of Hansen and Nielsen whereupon, in the case of methanol synthesis, an increasing CO2 concentration comes along with a decrease of maximum CO conversion and this does not necessarily lead to an irreversible impact on the catalyst system. Regarding direct DME synthesis, it was pointed out that the addition of CO2 to the gas feed can also considerably improve the long-term stability of catalyst systems.

Direct conversion of carbon-monoxide-rich synthesis gas to DME essentially depends on the acidity of the dehydration component in the catalyst system. If acidity is too low, the amount of methanol formed cannot be dehydrated with sufficient efficiency. If the acidity of the catalyst is too high, it also catalyzes further conversion of DME to hydrocarbons. During the investigation described here, γ-Al2O3 was found to be a suitable dehydration catalyst. A temperature increase up to 280°C, a higher content of H2 in the synthesis gas and a longer residence time lead to higher CO conversion. DME selectivity is mainly dependent on the type of dehydration catalyst and can be influenced by temperature and residence time, especially in the case of the dehydration catalysts H-MFI 90 and H-MOR 90. Studies on the impact of water on the catalyst system Cu/ZnO/Al2O3-γ-Al2O3 show that in the case of moderate water addition (<10%), neither the methanol or WGSR catalysts nor γ-Al2O3 exhibit rapid deactivation effects within several hours. While running the reaction for several days with water feeding of 10%, WGSR is the dominating reaction and CO2 formation is strongly enhanced at the expense of DME selectivity. Returning to the water-free operation mode causes decreasing activity in terms of CO conversion but high DME selectivity can be completely restored. Operation of the catalyst system in the presence of 8% of CO2 causes an approximately 10% lower CO conversion and an about 5% lower DME selectivity compared to the reaction system without CO2. Long-term investigations indicate reasonable catalytic performance over at least several weeks.
